title: Semisimplicity of a point is detected by a faithful rational representation
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $J$ be an affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Fix integers $m,d\geq1$ and homomorphisms of $k$-group schemes $i:J\to\operatorname{GL}_{m,k}$ and $r:J\to\operatorname{GL}_{d,k}$ [def-sc-general-linear-group]. Suppose $i$ is faithful: for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, the map $i_A:J(A)\to\operatorname{GL}_m(A)$ is injective, where $J(A)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}A,J)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. For every $g\in J(k)$, if the matrix $i_k(g)$ is diagonalizable over $k$, then the matrix $r_k(g)$ is diagonalizable over $k$. Here diagonalizable means conjugate by an invertible matrix over $k$ to a diagonal matrix. No smoothness, connectedness or characteristic-zero hypothesis on $J$ or $k$ is imposed.

source.place: Section 9.19, printed p.171 (semisimplicity in one faithful representation implies semisimplicity in all representations), with Theorem 9.18, printed p.170. Over an algebraically closed field, semisimple matrices are diagonalizable.

proof.text: For every finite-dimensional rational representation $(V,r_V)$ of $J$, put $A_V=r_V(g)$ and $\lambda_V=(A_V)_s$, using [lem-sfb-multiplicative-jordan-linear-compatibility]. These maps are invertible. Use the representations, equivariant maps, tensor action and unit specified in [lem-sfb-tannaka-rational-point-reconstruction]. For an equivariant $f:V\to W$, evaluation at the algebra $k$ and point $g$ gives $fA_V=A_Wf$; the intertwiner clause gives $f\lambda_V=\lambda_Wf$. The tensor clause gives $\lambda_{V\otimes W}=\lambda_V\otimes\lambda_W$. For the trivial representation, $A_{\mathbf1}=I$, whose decomposition $I=I\cdot I$ has diagonalizable first factor and $(I-I)^1=0$. Uniqueness gives $\lambda_{\mathbf1}=I$. The zero representation is allowed by both cited statements.

source.place: Theorem 9.18 proof, printed p.170; Propositions 9.13 and 9.15, printed p.169; Theorem 9.2 conditions (a)--(c), printed p.164.

proof.text: The family of step 1 satisfies all hypotheses of [lem-sfb-tannaka-rational-point-reconstruction]: $k$ is algebraically closed, $J$ is affine of finite type, and the maps are invertible, natural, tensor-compatible and the identity on the unit. Thus there exists $h\in J(k)$ such that $r_V(h)=(r_V(g))_s$ for every finite-dimensional rational representation. In particular, on $k^m$ and $k^d$ one obtains $i_k(h)=(i_k(g))_s$ and $r_k(h)=(r_k(g))_s$.

source.place: Theorem 9.18 proof, printed p.170, applying Theorem 9.2 to the family of semisimple parts.

proof.text: By hypothesis $i_k(g)$ is diagonalizable. Hence $i_k(g)=i_k(g)I_m=I_m i_k(g)$ is a decomposition with diagonalizable first factor and unipotent second factor, since $(I_m-I_m)^1=0$. Uniqueness in [lem-sfb-multiplicative-jordan-linear-compatibility] gives $(i_k(g))_s=i_k(g)$. Step 2 implies $i_k(h)=i_k(g)$. Apply faithfulness at the commutative $k$-algebra $k$ to conclude $h=g$.

source.place: Section 9.19, printed p.171; uniqueness of the matrix decomposition in Theorem 9.11, printed pp.168--169.

proof.text: Substitute $h=g$ into $r_k(h)=(r_k(g))_s$. The first factor supplied by [lem-sfb-multiplicative-jordan-linear-compatibility] is diagonalizable over $k$, so $r_k(g)$ is diagonalizable. No assertion about other points, smoothness or connectedness was used.

source.place: Section 9.19, printed p.171, conclusion in every representation.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 9.18 proof and Section 9.19, printed pp.170--171, using Theorem 9.2 and Propositions 9.13, 9.15.
